## R Markdown

This is an R Markdown document. Markdown is a simple formatting syntax for authoring HTML, PDF, and MS Word documents. For more details on using R Markdown see <http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com>.

When you click the **Knit** button a document will be generated that includes both content as well as the output of any embedded R code chunks within the document. You can embed an R code chunk like this:

```{r cars}
summary(cars)
```

## Including Plots

You can also embed plots, for example:

```{r pressure, echo=FALSE}
plot(pressure)
```

Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.

 ******* PART A - Creating Vectors: c(), seq(), rep() *******

```{r}

# spaced numbers between 0 and 1

1:19
seq(1, 19, by = 2) 
seq(0, 1, length.out = 5)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Use rep() to create a vector that repeats the value "A" 4 times

# TODO: Use rep() with the "each" argument to turn c("A", "B") into
# "A" "A" "B" "B" (each element repeated twice, in order)

# TODO: Use rep() with the "times" argument to turn c("A", "B") into
```

```{r}
#Question #1:

#Set up a vector named age, consisting of 15, 28, 32, 36, 27, 18, 52, 39, 42, 29, 35, 31, 27, 22, 37, 34, 19, 20, 57, 49, 50, 37, 46, 25, 17, 12, 42, 53, 41, 51, 35, 24, 33, 8.

age <- c(15, 28, 32, 36, 27, 18, 52, 39, 42, 29, 35, 31, 27, 22, 37, 34, 19, 20, 57, 49, 50, 37, 46, 25, 17, 12, 42, 53, 41, 51, 35, 24, 33, 8)

#a. How many data points?
length(age)
#Answer: 34 data points.

#b. Find the reciprocal of age?
1 / age
#Answer:[1] 0.06666667 0.03571429 0.03125000 0.02777778 0.03703704 0.05555556 0.01923077 0.02564103
#[9] 0.02380952 0.03448276 0.02857143 0.03225806 0.03703704 0.04545455 0.02702703 0.02941176
#[17] 0.05263158 0.05000000 0.01754386 0.02040816 0.02000000 0.02702703 0.02173913 0.04000000
#[25] 0.05882353 0.08333333 0.02380952 0.01886792 0.02439024 0.01960784 0.02857143 0.04166667
#[33] 0.03030303 0.12500000

#c. Assign also new_age <- c(age, 0, age). What happens to new_age?
new_age <- c(age, 0, age)
#Answer: the new_age has double the amount of data points as age plus 1 due to the number 0 adding 1 more value resulting to 68+1(the 0)= 69 total data points. 

#d. Find the minimum and the maximum value of age.
min(age) # 8
max(age) # 57
```

```{r}
#Question #3:

#Compare seq(1, 20, by = 2) with seq(1, 20, length.out = 5). What does each argument (by vs length.out) control, and when would you use one over the other in a real analysis?

#Answer: by is used to count each number up to the last one. If by > 1, say by = 2, then by will count the numbers by 2, which would skip other numbers. length.out on the other hand will calculate the spacing of each numbers up to reaching the value of 20 in this case. the spacing for each one is equal to one another. 

```

 ******* PART B - Subsetting (Accessing) Vectors *******
```{r}
grades <- c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84)
names(grades) <- c("Math", "Science", "English", "History", "PE")

# TODO: Access the 3rd element of grades using positional indexing
grades[3]

# TODO: Access the 1st abd 4th element of grades using positional indexing
grades[c(1, 4)]

# TODO: Access "Science" and "PE" together using their names
grades[c("Science", "PE")]

```
  
```{r}
# TODO: Return all elements of grades EXCEPT the 1st and 4th, using
# negative indexing, e.g. grades[-c(...)]

grades[-c(1, 4)]
```
  
```{r}
# TODO: Use a logical condition to return only the grades that are
# greater than or equal to 85 (hint: grades[grades >= 85])

grades[grades >= 85]
```
  
```{r}
#Question #5:

#Negative indexing (grades[-1]) removes an element, while logical indexing (grades[grades >= 85]) filters by a condition.

#Describe a real situation where you would need negative indexing, and a different situation where logical indexing would be the better tool.


#Answer: one of the examples where we can use logical indexing is when cleaning out missing data. It can be in a form of a survey, then use logical indexing to only get the data that respondents actually answered in the survey, while cleaning up the rest.

#As for negative indexing. One of its use case dropping a specific column when importing a spreadsheet into a matrix. This is useful if only a few specific columns are needed to run math on the data by omitting the irrelevant data.

``` 

```{r}
#Question #6:

#What happens if you run grades[10] (an index that doesn’t exist)? Run it, observe the result, and explain why R responds this way instead of throwing an error.


#Answer: The result is NA. In this specific code, it looks for an element in index 10, but there's no value and the current vector only spans up to 5 indexes with their respective values, hence it returns NA.

```

```{r}
#Question #7:

#Print a vector with the integers between 1 and 100 that are not divisible by 3, 5 and 7 using filter option.

#Write the R code and its output.

Filter(function(i) { all(i %% c(3,5,7) != 0) }, seq(100))

#Output:  [1]  1  2  4  8 11 13 16 17 19 22 23 26 29 31 32 34 37 38 41 43 44 46 47 52 53
#[26] 58 59 61 62 64 67 68 71 73 74 76 79 82 83 86 88 89 92 94 97
```

 *******PART C - Vector Operations and append()
```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
y <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)

# TODO: Add x and y element-wise, and print the result

sum_result <- x + y
print(sum_result)

# TODO: Multiply every element of x by 2

multiply_result <- x * 2
print(multiply_result)
```

```{r}
z <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
short <- c(1, 0)

# TODO: Add z and short together and print the result. Run this even
# though the vectors are different lengths -- observe what R does.

print(z + short)

```

```{r}
fruits <- c("apple", "banana", "cherry")

# TODO: Use append() to add "date" to the end of fruits

fruits <- append(fruits, "date")
print(fruits)

# TODO: Use append() with the "after" argument to insert "kiwi" between
# "apple" and "banana" (i.e., after position 1)

fruits <- append(fruits, "kiwi", after = 1)
print(fruits)

```

```{r}
#Question #8:

#In the vectors-recycling chunk, z has 6 elements and short has only 2. R still produced an answer instead of an error.

#Answer: R has vector recycling, where it repeats the elements in the shorter vector until it matches the length of the longer vector.


#Explain, in your own words, what R’s “recycling rule” did to short to make the addition work.

#Answer: R will add the elements of z and short starting from the very first element, down to the last one. If one vector is shorter than the other, the shorter vector will reach its last element first, then the addition will now go back to the first element of that vector to execute the addition until all the elements in the longer vector gets visited.
```

```{r}
#Question #9: Now try adding z (length 6) to c(1, 0, 1) (length 3) instead. Does it work cleanly?

result <- z + c(1, 0, 1)

print(result)

#Answer: Yes, it works cleanly, with no warnings since both z and c lengths are divisible.

#Then try adding z to c(1, 0, 1, 1) (length 4). Compare the warning (or lack of one) in each case, and explain what condition determines whether R recycles silently versus with a warning.

result <- z + c(1, 0, 1, 1)

print(result)

#Answer: the determining condition is whether both lengths of the two variables are multiples of one another, or divides with no decimal. If both variable lengths aren't multiples of one another, R will display an error, but still executes the code. 
```

******* PART D — Lists: Creating and Subsetting

```{r}
# TODO: Create a list called student with these named elements:
# name = "Maria Santos", age = 20, grades = c(88, 92, 79),
# is_enrolled = TRUE

student <- list(
name = "Maria Santos",
age = 20,
grades = c(88, 92, 79),
is_enrolled = TRUE
)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Access the "grades" element of student using single brackets
# student["grades"] -- then check its type with class()

student["grades"]
class(student)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Access the "grades" element of student using double brackets
# student[["grades"]] -- then check its type with class()

student[["grades"]]
class(student)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Access the "name" element of student using the $ operator
# student$name

student$name
```

```{r}
# TODO: From student, extract just the SECOND grade in the grades vector
# in a single expression, e.g. student[["grades"]][2] or student$grades[2]

student[["grades"]][2]
# or
student$grades[2]
```

```{r}
#Question #10:

#student["grades"] and student[["grades"]] look similar but return objects of different classes.

class(student["grades"])
class(student[["grades"]])


#Run class() on each and explain the difference in what single-bracket [ ] versus double-bracket [[ ]] return from a list.

#Answer: single bracket returns a value that belongs to a list, hence the value is classified as a "list". Double brackets on the other hand returns a value of that specific variable, such as grades being classified as numeric since it contains numeric values.

```
```{r}
#Question #11:

#Why do you think R makes a distinction between [ ] and [[ ]] for lists, but a vector only needs [ ]? Think about what a list can contain that a vector cannot.

#Answer: lists can contain variables of different types, such as numeric, strings, etc. A vector on the other hand can only contain a variable of a specific type, such as grades being numeric. If you declare grades in a vector, that vector must only contain numeric values.
```

******* PART E — Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
inventory <- list(
  item = c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"),
  price = c(25.50, 10.00, 5.00),
  in_stock = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

# TODO: Using what you learned in Parts B and D, print only the items
# (from inventory$item) that are currently in stock (in_stock == TRUE)

inventory$item[inventory$in_stock == TRUE]

```

```{r}
# TODO: A new product "Ruler" priced at 15.00 and in stock (TRUE) needs
# to be added to inventory. Use append() to add "Ruler" to
# inventory$item, 15.00 to inventory$price, and TRUE to inventory$in_stock.
# (You will need three separate append() calls, one per vector.)

inventory$item <- append(inventory$item, "Ruler")
inventory$price <- append(inventory$price, 15.00)
inventory$in_stock <- append(inventory$in_stock, TRUE)
```

```{r}
#Question #12:

#In challenge-1, you combined logical indexing on one vector (in_stock) to filter a different vector (item) inside the same list. Explain, step by step, why inventory$item[inventory$in_stock] works even though item and in_stock are stored as separate elements of the list.

#Answer:
#1. R evaluates the position of the elements in (in_stock) and (item) to determine the value that corresponds with a specific element.

#2. extract the logical vector for in_stock to get the TRUE values, while excluding the False values.

#3. extract the item vector for item to get the names of the items listed inside the vector.

#4. combine both operations to get the items that are in stock(TRUE).
```

```{r}
#Question #13:

#Suppose a classmate stores related data as three separate, unconnected vectors (item_names, item_prices, item_stock) instead of grouping them into one list like inventory. What risks or bugs could this create as the dataset grows or gets reordered? Argue for or against using a list (or, later, a data frame) instead of separate vectors.

#Answer: using separate vectors to store related data has a high risk of creating data misalignment 

```
